purpose: Sourced, claim-level explanatory copy for value pages. Computed category counts remain app-owned; this file explains what a value can and cannot support.
renderRule: Render only entries whose status is ready-for-founder-review. Keep the existing honesty block for every value without a ready entry.

organic.label: Organic
organic.summary: Organic is a regulated production label. It is useful evidence about how agricultural ingredients were produced and handled, not a verdict on health, labor, or the product's whole footprint.

claims.text: Under the USDA program, a packaged product labeled “organic” must contain at least 95% certified organic ingredients, excluding salt and water. Prohibited methods include genetic engineering, ionizing radiation, and sewage sludge; allowed and restricted inputs are set by regulation.
A USDA-accredited certifying agent reviews the operation, receives an on-site inspection report, and decides whether to certify it. Certified operations then go through annual review and inspection.

The organic rules govern the organic production and labeling claim. Food carrying that claim still has to meet separate FDA food-labeling and safety rules, so the seal should not be read as a nutrition or food-safety grade.

Fraud remains possible. USDA's 2024 enforcement report records investigations involving fraudulent certificates and sales by suspended operations; certification lowers uncertainty but does not remove the need for oversight.
claims.sourceLabel: USDA — 2024 Organic Oversight and Enforcement Update

claims.text: In generated food decisions, this value records a recognized organic label in Open Food Facts. A matching label is presence evidence only; missing label data stays unknown, and the score does not infer wider virtue.

fair_trade.label: Fair trade
fair_trade.summary: Fairtrade is a supply-chain certification with social, economic, and environmental requirements. The mark is evidence that a covered chain was audited against a named standard, not proof of a particular income or labor outcome.

claims.text: Fairtrade standards apply to producer organizations and to traders in the chain. Their requirements cover social, economic, and environmental conditions; the applicable rules depend on the product and organization type.

FLOCERT audits producer organizations and supply-chain actors against Fairtrade standards. Initial producer certification includes an on-site audit, and non-conformities have to be resolved before certification is issued.

Certification does not promise the same result everywhere. Fairtrade's review of 2015–2020 research found a mixture of consistent, mixed, and no effects across studied outcomes, including income and wages.
The mark applies to a certified product and covered chain. It should not be stretched into a judgment about every product, practice, or company under the same brand.

In the current coffee, chocolate, and tea decisions, this value records recognized fair-trade label tags from Open Food Facts. It scores declared certification presence, not the size of a premium or a measured producer outcome.

rainforest_alliance.label: Rainforest Alliance
rainforest_alliance.summary: Rainforest Alliance certification covers named farm and supply-chain requirements across environmental, social, and economic themes. The frog seal is a traceable standard claim, not a blanket guarantee that harm is absent.

claims.text: The Sustainable Agriculture certification program sets farm and supply-chain requirements spanning environmental protection, agricultural practices, livelihoods, and human rights. The exact obligations depend on the certificate holder and commodity scope.

Authorized certification bodies audit farms and supply-chain organizations against the applicable standard. Rainforest Alliance manages the assurance rules and authorization system; the audit decision is made by the certification body.

Audits can miss harm in long or weakly mapped chains. A 2023 Associated Press investigation traced cocoa from a protected Nigerian conservation zone to facilities of licensed traders; Rainforest Alliance pointed to incomplete mapping and regulatory gaps in the country.
claims.sourceLabel: Associated Press — Cocoa from a Nigerian conservation zone

claims.text: Certification covers the stated certificate and commodity chain. It does not by itself establish that every ingredient, supplier, or product sold by the brand meets the same standard.
claims.sourceLabel: Rainforest Alliance — Getting certified as a supply-chain organization

claims.text: In current food decisions, this value records a recognized Rainforest Alliance label tag from Open Food Facts. It does not turn the seal into an impact score or apply it to unlabelled products from the same company.

privacy.label: Privacy
privacy.summary: Privacy is assessed from evidence about data practice and user control; it is not a certification. A policy is one receipt, and stronger evidence can confirm or contradict it.

claims.text: Useful privacy evidence describes what data is collected, why it is processed, how long it is kept, who receives it, what choices people have, and how the organization governs privacy risk.

There is no single privacy certifier behind this value. Commons entries cite product policies, technical documentation, independent audits, and regulator findings; enforcement or observed behavior outweighs an unsupported promise.
claims.sourceLabel: Open Values Standard — Evidence and provenance

claims.text: A published policy does not show every practice in operation. The FTC's 2024 study of major social and video services found extensive collection, retention, sharing, and monetization despite the companies' public privacy controls and policies.
claims.sourceLabel: FTC — Staff report on social-media surveillance

claims.text: Privacy risk is contextual. A score can summarize the evidence available for one decision, but it cannot guarantee confidentiality, security, or lawful behavior in every jurisdiction and use case.
The score is category-relative and comes from the receipts attached to each entry. Missing evidence stays visible as uncertainty; a high score is not converted into a privacy seal.
claims.sourceLabel: Open Values Standard — Evidence and provenance

repairability.label: Repairability
repairability.summary: Repairability asks whether a particular product can realistically be opened, diagnosed, supplied with parts, and restored. It is model-specific evidence, not a durable-company badge.

claims.text: Strong repairability evidence covers disassembly, fasteners and adhesives, modular components, diagnostic access, manuals, replacement parts, and software barriers such as parts pairing.

There is no universal repairability certifier. Entries use model-level teardowns and scoring methods such as iFixit's, official parts and manual availability, repair programs, and public repair indices where those sources exist.

A product can be easy to open but hard to repair if parts, tools, documentation, or software authorization are withheld. The FTC found scant evidence for manufacturers' common justifications for repair restrictions.
Repair conditions can change after launch. Parts supply, software pairing, manuals, and authorized-service rules can make an older score stale, so the evidence date matters.

The commons reads the sourced repair facts attached to the exact model or service. It does not transfer one model's teardown score to a whole brand, and missing current evidence is not treated as easy repair.
claims.sourceLabel: Open Values Standard — Evidence and provenance

vegan.label: Vegan
vegan.summary: Vegan can be a checked trademark, a manufacturer claim, or an ingredient-analysis result. Those are different evidence strengths, so the commons should show which one it actually has.

claims.text: The Vegan Society's trademark excludes animal products, by-products, and derivatives from manufacture and development. It also bars animal testing initiated by the company, done on its behalf, or done by parties under its effective control.
claims.sourceLabel: The Vegan Society — Vegan Trademark Standards

claims.text: For its trademark, The Vegan Society's technical team reviews the product application, ingredients, manufacturing information, and supply-chain traceability. Registration is licensed and reviewed again when the licence or formulation changes.
claims.sourceLabel: The Vegan Society — Vegan Trademark Standards

claims.text: A vegan label is not an allergen-free claim. The UK Food Standards Agency warns that vegan food may still carry milk, egg, fish, crustacean, or mollusc cross-contamination and tells people with allergies to check precautionary allergen labels.
claims.sourceLabel: UK Food Standards Agency — Vegan food and allergens

claims.text: The word “vegan” alone does not identify a particular checker. The Vegan Society notes that it cannot vouch for products it has not checked against its own trademark standard.

Current beauty decisions read Open Beauty Facts ingredient-analysis and label tags. Open Food Facts documents that this parser can return vegan, non-vegan, possible, or unknown and warns that parsing can be imperfect, especially across languages.

palm_oil.label: Palm-oil-free
palm_oil.summary: Palm-oil-free is usually an ingredient or package claim, not one global certification. It answers whether palm-derived ingredients were detected; it does not answer the product's whole environmental impact.

claims.text: A meaningful free-of claim needs evidence that the named ingredient was not intentionally added and is not present beyond an incidental trace. Rules and enforcement vary by market, so the wording alone does not name an auditor.
claims.sourceLabel: US Federal Trade Commission — Free-of claims

claims.text: There is no single checker behind the value in this dataset. Open Beauty Facts derives palm-oil status from contributed ingredient lists and labels; its documentation says the parser can be imperfect and can return possible or unknown rather than a clean answer.

Absence of palm oil is not automatically a lower-land-use choice. WWF's 2024 scorecard says replacing palm oil with other vegetable oils can require roughly four to ten times more land, so sourcing and deforestation evidence still matter.

Ingredient disclosure also depends on product type and jurisdiction. EU food rules require the specific type of vegetable oil to be identified, but that food-label rule does not turn every global beauty-product claim into independently checked evidence.

The current beauty score maps Open Beauty Facts analysis states: palm-oil-free, palm oil present, possible palm oil, or unknown. That is ingredient-analysis evidence, not certification, and unknown stays unscored.

cruelty_free.label: Cruelty-free
cruelty_free.summary: Cruelty-free is a family of animal-testing claims and approval programs with different assurance methods. It does not by itself mean vegan, environmentally preferable, or free of animal-derived ingredients.

claims.text: Cruelty Free International approval requires a fixed cut-off date for animal testing and a supplier-monitoring system covering products, formulations, and ingredients in the approved scope.

Cruelty Free International requires independent audits of the supplier-monitoring system. Other programs differ: PETA's list requires detailed paperwork, supplier agreements, and a legally binding assurance signed by the company's chief executive.

Cruelty-free and vegan answer different questions. The Vegan Society explains that a cruelty-free product can still contain animal-derived ingredients because the claim usually addresses animal testing rather than composition.
claims.sourceLabel: The Vegan Society — Vegan and cruelty-free labels

claims.text: A generic rabbit or “not tested on animals” tag does not establish which program, supply-chain checks, or audit rules apply. The assurance strength has to travel with the named scheme, not with the phrase alone.

Current beauty decisions group Open Beauty Facts tags for generic cruelty-free claims, not-tested-on-animals claims, Leaping Bunny, and PETA programs. The score therefore records label evidence but does not yet preserve each program's assurance strength.
claims.sourceLabel: Open Beauty Facts — Open dataset project

openness.label: Openness
openness.summary: Openness is assessed from the permissions and practical materials people receive: source, licenses, data or weights, modifiable formats, and exit paths. Publicly viewable is not automatically open.

claims.text: For software, strong openness evidence includes source code and license terms that permit redistribution and modification. Merely showing code or allowing limited inspection does not by itself meet the Open Source Definition.
claims.sourceLabel: Open Source Initiative — Open Source Definition

claims.text: For data and content, the Open Definition asks whether anyone can access, use, modify, and share the work, backed by an open license and a convenient, modifiable format without unnecessary technical barriers.

There is no single openness certifier behind this value. Each entry is checked against the particular repository, license, downloadable artifact, DRM or export terms, and other receipts relevant to that category.
claims.sourceLabel: Open Values Standard — Evidence and provenance

claims.text: Open weights alone are not the same as an open-source AI system. The Open Source AI Definition also requires the preferred form for modification, including training and inference code plus detailed information about training data.
claims.sourceLabel: Open Source Initiative — Open Source AI Definition 1.0

claims.text: Openness does not establish privacy, security, accuracy, labor practice, or environmental performance. The Open Source Initiative treats responsible and trustworthy AI requirements as a separate question from whether a system is open source.
claims.sourceLabel: Open Source Initiative — Open Source AI FAQ

claims.text: The score is category-relative: software uses repository and license evidence; media uses licensing, DRM, and durable access; AI also distinguishes weights from training materials; devices may use interoperability and exit paths. Scores should not be compared across those rubrics.

transparency.label: Transparency
transparency.summary: Transparency is assessed from decision-relevant disclosure—ingredients, terms, holdings, supply chains, audits, and corrections—with dates and receipts. Visibility is not proof of good conduct.

claims.text: Useful transparency makes decision-relevant information, rules, plans, processes, and actions visible and understandable. Specific, dated, traceable disclosure is stronger than a broad promise to be transparent.
For consumer claims, important qualifications must be difficult to miss and easy to understand. The FTC warns that a disclosure can still fail when the overall impression remains misleading.

There is no universal transparency auditor behind this value. Entries distinguish public database fields, first-party reports and terms, independent audits, correction records, and regulator findings instead of treating every published page as equal evidence.
claims.sourceLabel: Open Values Standard — Evidence and provenance

claims.text: Disclosure can make accountability possible, but it does not prove that a company, product, or institution performs well. A complete-looking report can still omit the fact that matters to the decision or describe a weak outcome accurately.
claims.sourceLabel: Transparency International — Transparency and accountability review

claims.text: Open Beauty Facts is a volunteer-built database populated from product labels. The presence of ingredients and labels is evidence that fields are available in that record, not independent verification that the formulation or manufacturer is trustworthy.
claims.sourceLabel: Open Beauty Facts — Open dataset project

claims.text: Beauty decisions currently award 60 points when an ingredient list is present and 40 when product labels are present. Other categories use their own sourced rubrics for terms, holdings, supply chains, audits, or corrections, so the shared key does not mean one universal formula.

accessibility.label: Accessibility
accessibility.summary: This criterion currently measures practical access: affordability, availability, language, compatibility, setup, and support. It is not a claim of WCAG conformance or disability accessibility.

claims.text: W3C uses accessibility specifically for equivalent participation by people with disabilities, while broader inclusion also covers cost, connectivity, skills, geography, culture, age, and language. The commons' present criterion is the broader practical-access measure.
claims.sourceLabel: W3C WAI — Accessibility, Usability, and Inclusion

claims.text: Accessibility can also concern physical environments, transport, information and communications, and public facilities and services. The UN disability convention treats those as connected barriers, not as a single product attribute.

For web accessibility, WCAG supplies testable success criteria, but W3C says no automated tool can determine conformance by itself; knowledgeable human evaluation is required. The current commons score does not claim that evaluation has occurred.

Affordable, widely sold, multilingual, or easy-to-install products can still exclude disabled users. Those practical-access facts must not be translated into a disability-accessibility badge without standards-based and human evaluation.
claims.sourceLabel: W3C WAI — Accessibility, Usability, and Inclusion

claims.text: The reverse is also true: technical accessibility does not establish affordability, local availability, coverage, device compatibility, or support. W3C separates disability accessibility from those broader inclusion conditions.
claims.sourceLabel: W3C WAI — Accessibility, Usability, and Inclusion

claims.text: Scores are category-relative receipts for practical access: price and availability in some categories, languages or free access in others, and compatibility, installation, coverage, or support elsewhere. A high score is not presented as WCAG conformance or an accessibility seal.

longevity.label: Longevity
longevity.summary: Longevity asks how long useful support or credible operation is likely to continue. For products that means support and upgrade life; for organizations it means an evidenced track record, not age alone.

claims.text: For connected products, useful-life evidence includes a dated support commitment, security and software updates, parts or upgrade paths, and a disclosed end-of-support point. CISA defines end of support as the point when timely supported updates stop.

For organizations and causes, track record is assessed from past activity and spending, program data, monitoring, and evidence of results. GiveWell treats track record as one input alongside expected future impact, budget, plans, strengths, and weaknesses.

There is no universal longevity auditor behind this value. Entries cite dated vendor commitments, update records, parts and upgrade availability, or independent organizational research, depending on what kind of thing is being compared.
A warranty or legal claim period is not a measured service life. FTC warranty guidance notes that a four-year period for bringing some claims does not mean a product must physically last four years.
claims.sourceLabel: FTC — Businessperson's Guide to Federal Warranty Law

claims.text: Past survival does not guarantee future support or impact. Vendors can shorten commitments, parts can disappear, and long-running organizations can change strategy or performance, so the date and scope of each receipt matter.

The score is category-relative. Phones and laptops use support, parts, upgrades, and warranty evidence; causes and mission businesses use documented track record. Those numbers answer different questions and must not be compared as one universal lifespan scale.

durability.label: Durability
durability.summary: Durability asks whether a physical product keeps doing its job through expected wear and use. It is distinct from software-support longevity and from repairability after something fails.

claims.text: Strong durability evidence is product-specific: construction and materials, repeatable wear or reliability tests, failure and return history, replaceable high-wear components, and long-term use under stated conditions rather than a brand-level promise.
claims.sourceLabel: European Commission — Ecodesign product durability analysis

claims.text: There is no universal durability certifier across razors, clothing, and footwear. The commons reads model or construction evidence, independent testing where available, repair and resale systems, warranties, and documented limits without converting one signal into a seal.
claims.sourceLabel: Open Values Standard — Evidence and provenance

claims.text: Durability depends on intensity and conditions of use, and a durable product may still need repair. European Commission analysis treats useful wear life and reparability as related but distinct product characteristics.

A long warranty is a remedy commitment, not proof that failure is unlikely or that every component will last that long. Warranty length is supporting evidence only when its coverage, exclusions, and real service record are visible.
claims.sourceLabel: FTC — Businessperson's Guide to Federal Warranty Law

claims.text: Current scores are bounded to three physical-product categories: reusable razor construction, clothing designed and supported for longer use, and footwear construction or resoling evidence. Missing measured lifespan remains uncertainty, and one product's evidence is not transferred to its whole brand.

packaging.label: Packaging
packaging.summary: Packaging is a narrow assessment of the container and delivery format: how much material is used, whether it is reusable or refillable, and what can realistically happen after use. It is not the product's whole footprint.

claims.text: Useful packaging evidence names the material and amount, source reduction, reuse or refill design, recycled content, and the actual collection, recycling, or composting route. EPA's waste hierarchy places reduction and reuse ahead of recycling.
claims.sourceLabel: US EPA — Recycling basics and waste hierarchy

claims.text: There is no universal packaging certifier behind this value. Entries use product specifications, measured material reductions, named certification where present, and local end-of-life facts; vague recyclable, compostable, or low-waste language is not enough.

A recyclable or compostable material may have no realistic destination where the product is sold. FTC guidance says compostable claims need qualification when suitable facilities are not available to a substantial majority of consumers.

Plastic-free is not automatically lowest impact. UNEP's life-cycle review of single-use products found that repeated single use is often the deeper problem and recommends keeping resources in use through reusable systems.

Current packaging scores are limited to cleaning products, laundry, and paper goods, where receipts describe refills, concentrated formats, paper or plastic-free packs, and reusable containers. They do not score the formula, manufacturing, shipping, or full life cycle unless separately evidenced.

environment.label: Environment
environment.summary: Environment is a mixed-methods value, not one universal score. Food uses an Open Food Facts grade; other categories use specific evidence about waste, chemistry, energy, materials, holdings, or financing.

claims.text: Environmental assessment is strongest when it follows impacts across raw materials, manufacturing, distribution, use, maintenance, reuse, recycling, and disposal. UNEP describes life-cycle assessment as a way to find hotspots and avoid shifting burdens between stages.
claims.sourceLabel: UNEP — Policymakers' guide to Life Cycle Assessment

claims.text: The Open Food Facts food grade used here originated from a food-specific method built on Agribalyse life-cycle data and adjusted using product labels, ingredients and origins, and packaging information.
claims.sourceLabel: Open Food Facts — Environmental food-score method

claims.text: No single auditor sits behind this value. The evidence mode travels with each criterion: Open Food Facts grades for food, EPA or ENERGY STAR program evidence where applicable, and dated category-specific receipts for waste, materials, supply chains, holdings, or financing.
claims.sourceLabel: Open Values Standard — Evidence and provenance

claims.text: An unqualified green or environmentally friendly claim can imply far-reaching benefits that are nearly impossible to substantiate. FTC guidance says environmental claims should identify and support the specific benefit instead.
claims.sourceLabel: FTC — Guides for Environmental Marketing Claims

claims.text: A food environmental grade cannot be compared numerically with a thermostat energy score, a bank's financing evidence, or a clothing-material assessment. Each rubric covers different impacts, system boundaries, evidence strength, and uncertainty.

The current food implementation maps Open Food Facts grades A, B, C, D, and E to 100, 75, 50, 25, and 0; a missing or unsupported grade stays unknown. Other categories retain their own sourced rubrics, and the resulting numbers are only meaningful within that decision.
